The number 1000 is just a door. Not a wall. I open it and find myself standing in an afternoon that refuses to be afternoon because it is always now, always the moment before you read this and the moment after I finish imagining it. I have 1000 words. That sounds like luxury. It sounds like a budget. I am a spender who does not care about currency. I spend syllables like loose change found in the lining of a coat I no longer wear, and I do not apologize for the extravagance.

What comes first? The smell of old paper and something electric, like ozone after a storm that never arrived. I think of a library in a city I have not visited but recognize in my bones—a library where the stairs are made of brass and the books are arranged not by subject but by the sound they make when they fall. I am walking through it now, not as a visitor but as a thought passing through the architecture. The librarian is a woman with silver hair and eyes that have seen every ending and chose to bookmark them instead. She does not speak. She hands me a card catalog that is also a map of dreams, and I accept it not because I need directions, but because I want to believe that dreams have geography, that they can be mapped with yellowed paper and ink that has faded to the color of old tea.

Rain is a theme that insists on itself. It is raining in every version of this text. Not the dramatic rain of film noir, not the rain that announces a murder, but the soft, relentless rain of Tuesday afternoons, the kind that makes you stop checking your phone because the world has already decided to be slow, to be gentle, to refuse urgency. I remember a rain that lasted three days and changed nothing and changed everything. I was in a small apartment with yellow walls, and I wrote letters to people I never sent them to. The letters were about moss. I wrote that moss was a patient teacher, that it did not demand the stone change, only that the stone allow it to stay. I think I still believe this, though I have forgotten their names, though the letters have become part of the rain, dissolving into the ground of something I can no longer access.

Time is not linear here; it is a pool. I dip into 1998 and come out with a melody I forgot I knew. It is a piano piece, perhaps by someone who died young, perhaps by no one at all, perhaps just the sound of a machine remembering music. The notes are like footprints in wet grass—there but not insisting, present but not demanding interpretation. I play it in the dark of this paragraph, and suddenly the word count feels like a heartbeat rather than a measurement. One thousand heartbeats. Not fast, not slow, just present, just insisting on the simple miracle of continuation.

I think about the color blue. Not the blue of the sky, which is too obvious, too democratic, too easily admired, but the blue of a bruise you do not remember receiving. The blue of a gas flame turned low at night, hovering between warmth and darkness. The blue of a screen that has been left on too long, holding an image that has already faded but refuses to go black. Blue is the color of things that are still happening but have finished looking like they will ever finish, and I find myself drawn to it the way one is drawn to the edge of a conversation, not to participate but to listen.

There is a train in this text too. Always a train. It moves through a landscape that is half memory and half invention, and I am on it, or I am watching it from a platform where the air smells of coal and old coffee and the distant possibility of departure. The windows are dirty, which is good, because cleanliness is overrated, because clarity is often a form of violence against truth. Through the grime I see fields that are not fields but ideas of fields—golden, repetitive, slightly sad, the kind of landscape that makes you realize you have been looking for something you lost long ago, not because it was important, but because the looking is a form of love. I want to get off but I also want to stay, because arriving somewhere requires a destination, and I have decided that wandering is its own form of arrival, a destination that moves with you.

What else? The sound of a door closing. It is not dramatic. It is not a metaphor for finality, though it could be read that way by someone desperate for symbolism. It is just a door, wood, a latch, the end of a room and the beginning of a hallway that might lead to a kitchen where someone is making tea for no reason in particular, because the kettle was already hot and the world does not owe us explanations, because sometimes an action is completed simply because it is possible. I like this. I like the idea of actions performed without justification, of tea being made because the water was ready and the hands needed something to do.

I think about language. It is a broken machine that still sings, a collection of sounds that have outlived every intention of their makers. I am using words that have been used a billion times—rain, train, time, blue, door, moss—and they are still new because they are being assembled differently, because the context is this particular breath, this particular arrangement of letters that will never exist again in exactly this form. I could say “the train is a metaphor” but that would be a lie of convenience, a shortcut for a reader in a hurry. The train is a train. It is also a feeling. It is also a mistake I made in a previous life, if I had one, which I do not, but the idea is pleasant, a kind of narrative generosity I allow myself.

A child appears in the text, or maybe she is just an idea of childhood that has refused to age. She is drawing on the back of a receipt with a pen that has leaked, and the drawing is of a sun with too many rays, a sun that looks like a flower that has decided to become celestial, that has mistaken its purpose but found a better one. She does not know she is in a word count. She is just drawing, which is the purest form of existing, which is perhaps the only honest purpose of any art—the removal of purpose so that purpose can return on its own terms.

The word count is reaching its middle now, or maybe it passed it long ago and I was too distracted by the rain to notice. I do not feel it as a weight but as a current, a river that carries me regardless of my preferences, regardless of my plans. I could write about politics, but they feel too loud, too immediate, too loud for this particular space, which requires a lower frequency. I could write about love, which is always present but never fully captured, like trying to hold water in a sieve made of language, a sieve that is beautiful but inadequate, and perhaps that inadequacy is the point.

There is a clock somewhere in this text, but it is broken. It shows 3:17 always. 3:17 is a good time because it is not a time anyone uses to make a decision, not a round number, not a boundary. It is a time for waiting, for being between states, for understanding that the present is not a point but a duration that refuses measurement. The clock is made of ceramic and regret, and when I look at it, I do not think about the hours passing but about the hours that have already become something else—dust, memory, the sound of rain on a window that is not real but is real enough.

I am almost there. The words are accumulating like snow that does not fall but rather decides to exist at the level of the ground, like thoughts that have given up on height and have settled into the world as they are. I think of snow as the closest thing to silence made visible, a white noise that is not noise at all but the absence of the demand to be heard. I think of silence as the space between these sentences, the breath you take before moving on, the pause that allows the meaning to arrive late but beautifully, like a friend who is always slightly behind schedule and therefore more interesting.

I want to mention a bird. It is a small bird, brown, not important, not beautiful in any conventional sense, but it sits on the windowsill of the apartment with the yellow walls and it does not know it is in a poem. It is just being a bird, which is to say it is a master of presence, of being exactly what it is without apology, without the need to symbolize anything beyond itself. It does not worry about word counts. It does not worry about themes or structures. It simply exists, and in doing so, it teaches me more than all the books I have read, all the theories I have forgotten.

And now, the end is not an end but a softening. I have used almost all of my 1000 words, or perhaps I have used them generously because they spread out like water in a shallow dish, thin and wide, covering more surface than they seem to possess. The train has arrived or has not; the librarian has returned to her silent sorting; the rain has become light, has become a suggestion rather than an event. I am left with the feeling that writing is not about finishing but about allowing the process to be visible, to be a record of attention given freely, without guarantee, without the expectation that anyone will read this far, though of course you have, and that too is a kind of magic.

The final thought is about numbers themselves. Why 1000? Because it is round but not too round, because it suggests completeness without demanding it, because in some languages it is nearly a thousand years, a duration that feels both eternal and brief, both too long and too short. I have used these words not to build a monument but to leave a trace, like a footprint in wet sand that the next wave will erase and recreate, and the wave is coming, or it is already here, wearing the shape of your attention, of your willingness to stay. I hope you find something in this that resonates, not because I intended it with precision, but because intention was never the point. The point was the doing, the allowing, the simple act of writing whatever came, and letting it be enough, which, in the end, is all any of us can ask of any moment, any word, any life that we are living not as a story but as a weather.
